title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — syllogism; limitatio; gratia
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. Why he calls this reason third, when it is fifth, I see no cause, except that, having passed over two, the second and the fourth, he yet did not wish to seem to have omitted any. I had also confirmed the minor of this fifth argument with four reasons: of which he objects to himself only the prior two, but so contracted, especially the first, that I scarcely recognize it. But he brings two replies by which he seems rather to strengthen the argument than to weaken it. By the prior he gives the reason why Adam was not damned. He therefore concedes (which was the confirmation of the minor of my argument) that he was not damned. For so my argument stood; If the law was threatening Adam with death situated in privation of justice, Adam was punished according to the law's threat. But Adam was not punished according to the law's threat. Therefore the Law was not threatening Adam with death situated in privation of justice. What does the Learned Man reply to the Major? Does he deny it? Does he distinguish? Does he apply a limitation to it? He replies nothing at all. He therefore concedes it. So it seems. Yet it can be limited: for since besides that privation the law was also threatening bodily and eternal death, Adam according to the law's threat would have been partly punished, partly not: he would have been punished by that privation or spiritual death, would not have been punished by bodily and eternal death. But this limitation does the argument no harm. For he would at least have been punished by some punishment properly so called, or judicial, which the Law was threatening, and indeed the greatest punishment. But that is false. For God granted him grace of the sin. But he is not punished to whom sin is remitted, to whom sin is not imputed, who has been justified from sin. For if he were partly punished, partly not, also to him sin would partly be remitted, partly not, and he would partly be justified, partly not; and justification would be imperfect, which no one of the Evangelicals would say. Since such is my argument, you see, reader, that this prior reply of the Learned Man shakes neither its major nor its minor. Let him proceed therefore.
pass_b_english: Placeus. Why call this the third reason when it is the fifth? I see no cause except that, having skipped the second and fourth, he still did not want to seem to have skipped any. I had backed this fifth argument's minor with four reasons; he takes up only the first two, so compressed—especially the first—that I scarcely know them. His two replies seem to shore the argument up more than tear it down.

The first explains why Adam was not damned—and so grants what confirmed my minor: he was not damned. My argument ran: If the law threatened Adam with death as privation of righteousness, Adam was punished as the law threatened. But he was not. Therefore the Law did not threaten him with that death. What does Garissoles say to the major? Deny? Distinguish? Limit? Nothing at all—so he concedes it.

One might limit: besides that privation the law also threatened bodily and eternal death, so Adam would have been partly punished (by spiritual death) and partly not (by bodily and eternal). The limit does not hurt the argument. He would still have been hit by some punishment properly so called—judicial, and the greatest—which the Law threatened. That is false. God granted him grace for the sin. The one whose sin is remitted, not imputed, who is justified from sin, is not punished. Partial punishment would mean partial remission and partial justification—an imperfect justification no evangelical would own. So, reader, this first reply shakes neither major nor minor. Let him go on.
source_text: PLAC. Cur hanc rationem, cum sit quinta, tertiam vocet, causam nullam video, nisi quia, cum duas praeterierit, secundam & quartam, videri tamen noluit ullam praetermisisse. Quatuor etiam rationibus minorem hujus argumenti quinti confirmaveram: ex quibus solas priores duas sibi objicit, sed ita contractas, praesertim primam, ut vix eam agnoscam. Adhibet autem responsiones duas, quibus argumentum firmare potius videtur, quam infirmare. Priore rationem reddit, cur Adamus non fuerit damnatus. Concedit igitur, (quae minoris argumenti mei confirmatio erat) eum non fuisse damnatum. Sic enim se habebat argumentum meum; Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae comminabatur, Adamus secundum legis comminationem punitus est. Atqui Adamus secundum legis comminationem punitus non est. Ergo Lex non comminabatur Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae. Quid respondet Vir Doctus ad Majorem? Num eam negat? Num distinguit? Num ei limitationem adhibet? Nihil prorsus respondet. Eam igitur concedit. Ita videtur. Potest tamen limitari: cum enim praeter illam privationem, etiam corporis & aeternam mortem lex minaretur, Adamus secundum legis comminationem partim punitus fuisset, partim non fuisset: Punitus fuisset illa privatione seu morte spirituali, non fuisset punitus morte corporis & aeterna. Sed haec limitatio argumento nihil nocet. Punitus enim saltem fuisset poena aliqua proprie dicta, seu judiciaria quam Lex comminabatur, & quidem poena maxima. Id autem est falsum. Fecit enim ei Deus gratiam peccati. Non punitur autem cui peccatum remittitur, cui peccatum non imputatur, qui justificatus est a peccato. Nam si partim puniretur, partim non puniretur, etiam ei partim peccatum remitteretur, partim non remitteretur, & partim justificaretur, partim non justificaretur; imperfectaque esset justificatio, id quod Evangelicorum nemo dixerit. Cum tale sit argumentum meum, vides, lector, hanc priorem Viri Docti responsionem illius neque majorem, neque minorem labefactare. Pergat igitur.

choices.choice: syllogism intact; limitatio fails; grace ⇒ not punished
